title: In Silico assessment of rat NOAEL using CORAL
content:
Abstract
The No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) is a critical metric for evaluating subchronic oral safety in rat models, representing the highest administered dose at which no adverse effects of tested chemicals are observed. The shift toward animal-free safety assessment has increased the demand for predictive computational models that can replicate biological endpoints with high fidelity. This study aims to develop QSAR models to predict the subchronic toxicity of structurally diverse organic compounds following repeated-dose exposure in rat models. The negative decimal logarithm of NOAEL served as the dependent variable. A Monte Carlo technique, integrated with a Las Vegas algorithm, was applied to build the models. Optimal descriptors were computed using attribute correlation weights derived from SMILES representations. Because optimizing these weights—and the resulting statistical quality—inherently depends on the data partitioning, this study evaluates whether the training-validation split can be optimized. Furthermore, it addresses the internal structure of the training set by partitioning it into three distinct subsets: active training, passive training, and calibration sets. Generalizations are based on the systematic examination of 100 splits generated via the Las Vegas algorithm into four subsets: active training, passive training, calibration, and validation sets. This probabilistic framework shifts QSAR interpretation from a static accuracy check to a novel diagnostic perspective, enabling the redefinition of data quality and the reevaluation of specific molecular potentials.
